subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If f(x) = 1 + x + x² + ⋯ + xⁿ, find f′(1).

mark_split.label: Write f′(x) with a general last term
Set x = 1 and give the answer as a formula in n

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what f′(x) looks like in general and why x = 1 leaves only the coefficients.

steps.label: Write f′(x) with a general last term
steps.margin_note: First mark. The working is the same as for a numbered case, but the last term must be carried as nxⁿ⁻¹ rather than a number. Keep the letter n right through — the question asks for a formula, not a value.
steps.memory_tip: The number of terms in f′ is n, not n + 1: the constant 1 in f contributes nothing.
lines: Using d/dx(xᵏ) = kxᵏ⁻¹ on each of the n + 1 terms,
So f′ has exactly n terms, with coefficients 1, 2, 3, …, n.

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = 1 + 2x + 3x² + ⋯ + nxⁿ⁻¹, carrying n as a letter.

the constant gives zero so there are n terms in the derivative

steps.why: A general question is marked on the general line. Replacing n by a chosen number such as 5 answers a different question and earns nothing.
common_mistakes: Writing the last derivative term as nxⁿ instead of nxⁿ⁻¹.
Saying f′ has n + 1 terms, by counting the constant 1, whose derivative is 0.

steps.label: Set x = 1 and give the answer as a formula in n
steps.margin_note: Second mark. At x = 1 every power is 1, so f′(1) is the sum of the coefficients 1, 2, …, n. That sum is the standard result n(n+1)/2 and stays a formula, not a number.
steps.memory_tip: Test any general answer on a small case. For n = 3, f′(1) = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 and n(n+1)/2 = 3 × 4/2 = 6.
lines: Put x = 1. Every power of 1 equals 1, so each term reduces to its coefficient.
This is the sum of the first n natural numbers.
Check with n = 3: f′(1) = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 and n(n+1)/2 = 6.

steps.why: The sum of the first n natural numbers is a standard result the student already has from Maths-1A, so quoting it finishes the question in one line.
common_mistakes: Giving a number such as 5050 when the question carries a general n.
Using (n−1)n/2, by summing to n − 1 because the last power shown is n − 1.
